items.title: fix(launchers): a Python repin retires the running Windows launcher
items.content:
fix(launchers): a Python repin retires the running Windows launcher

On Windows without distlib in the runtime environment, a repin of PM's Python
republishes the source launcher as a .cmd and must retire the old hermes.exe
so it cannot shadow it. stage_launcher deleted it, but the exe it has to
retire is usually the one running `hermes update` (or the launch retrying
the owed step), and Windows refuses to delete a mapped image. The publication
failed, the update owed 'launchers', so the install stamp and bootstrap
receipt were withheld at the old commit and the old exe kept booting the old
interpreter. Every retry ran from that same exe and failed the same way.

Windows does allow renaming a running image, so retire it by renaming it
aside when the delete fails (distlib's .deleteme move), and collect the aside
copy on a later publication once its process has exited.

Seen in the v0.22.5 rc.1 install E2E: installer-script -> hermes-update
(v0.22.4 -> HEAD) on Windows, where pm/lock.json moved Python 3.14.7 ->
3.14.9 (e31fa4cab92): "Update follow-up 'launchers' did not finish: source
launcher publication failed", then verify-stamp "pinnedCommit 4d04303818b6
!= installed HEAD 7c0905a00899".

items.title: Hermes Agent MCP Server: Use Hermes Inside Claude Code and Cursor
items.content:
Hermes Agent MCP server mode flips Hermes around. Normally you plug MCP servers into Hermes. With the mcp-serve plugin, Hermes itself becomes an MCP server, so Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or Codex can talk to it. It landed as an official plugin in Hermes Agent v0.22.4 on 21 October 2026. In the video below I show how I use MCP to give all my agents one shared memory across devices. Here’s what the Hermes MCP server does, how to set it up and what to watch out for.

Key takeaways

hermes mcp-serve turns Hermes into an MCP server.
Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and Codex can read and send your Hermes messages.
Add --tools to share web, browser, vision, image, skills and voice tools.
Terminal, file and kanban tools are never exposed. Claim a free strategy session for help.






What the Hermes Agent MCP server does
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way AI apps share tools. Hermes has long been an MCP client — you connect MCP servers to it (see my Hermes Agent MCP guide). The new mcp-serve plugin makes Hermes an MCP server too.
Run hermes mcp-serve and any MCP client can, over stdio:

List and read your messaging conversations (Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord and the rest).
Poll live events as they arrive.
Send messages through your connected accounts.
Answer approvals that Hermes is waiting on.

So you can sit in Claude Code or Cursor and say “check my Hermes messages and reply to the client who asked about pricing” — without switching apps.




Hermes MCP server at a glance





Command
hermes mcp-serve


Plugin
mcp-serve (official tier, v1.0.0)


Needs
Hermes Agent v0.22.0 or later


Clients
Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex — any MCP client


Transport
stdio


Optional
--tools exposes extra Hermes tools




Sharing Hermes tools with –tools
By default only the messaging features are shared. Add --tools and Hermes also exposes its web, browser, vision, image generation, skills and text-to-speech tools. That means Claude Code could use Hermes’ browser or your Hermes skills without setting them up twice.
Nous deliberately never exposes the terminal, file or kanban tools this way, so an outside client can’t run commands or edit files through Hermes.

How to set up the Hermes Agent MCP server

Update Hermes: hermes update.
Install the plugin: hermes plugins install mcp-serve.
Add Hermes to your MCP client with the command hermes and the argument mcp-serve (add --tools if you want the extra tools).
Restart the client and ask it to list your Hermes conversations.

A typical client config looks like this:
{ "mcpServers": { "hermes": { "command": "hermes", "args": ["mcp-serve"] } } }
Upgrading from an older setup? This used to be built into the core as hermes mcp serve (two words). Nous says MCP clients should change their args to ["mcp-serve"].
Security: what you’re handing over

Be clear about the access. The connecting client can read your active profile’s conversation history and send messages as your connected accounts. With –tools it also runs Hermes tools using your provider credentials, which can spend credits. Only connect clients you trust, and keep approvals on.

Why the Hermes MCP server matters
The biggest headache with running several agents is that each one lives in its own bubble. One has your messages, another has your code, another has your memory. MCP is how you break those walls down. That’s exactly why my Agent OS connects Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw and OpenCode to one shared memory and one set of skills.
With the Hermes MCP server, your coding agent can now reach the agent that talks to your customers and team. That’s the start of a real AI team, rather than a set of separate tools. For more on pairing them, see connect Hermes Agent to Claude Code.
Hermes MCP server vs Hermes as an MCP client





Hermes as MCP client
Hermes as MCP server




Direction
Other tools plug into Hermes
Hermes plugs into other apps


Use it to
Give Hermes new abilities (GitHub, Notion, databases)
Use Hermes’ messages and tools from Claude Code, Cursor or Codex


Setup
MCP servers listed in Hermes config.yaml
hermes mcp-serve in your client’s config




Hermes MCP server use cases

Customer replies from your editor — ask Claude Code to read new Hermes messages and draft replies while you code.
Approvals from anywhere — answer the approvals Hermes is waiting on without opening Hermes.
Shared browser and vision tools — with –tools, Cursor or Codex can use Hermes’ browser and image tools.
Reusing your skills — skills you’ve built in Hermes become available to other agents.
Live event feeds — poll new messages so a coding agent can react to a team request.

Start with read-only jobs like summarising conversations, then move to sending messages once you trust the setup.
My verdict on the Hermes Agent MCP server
This is one of the most useful plugins in the catalog for anyone running more than one agent. Coding agents get access to your messages and approvals, and Hermes’ tools become reusable everywhere. Connect only clients you trust, and the Hermes Agent MCP server ties your whole AI stack together.

items.content:
fix(launchers): every publication collects retired launcher copies

Review follow-up: the sweep of `hermes.exe.<pid>.deleteme` copies ran only
when the publication fell back to a .cmd launcher, so a later publication
with distlib available (an .exe) left the aside copy behind forever. The
sweep now runs on every successful publication. The running-launcher test
bounds its readiness wait, keeps the child's whole lifetime inside the
try/finally (kill + reap on a stuck shutdown), and republishes with distlib
restored to pin the collection.

Hermes Agent Microsoft Store app is the easiest way to get Hermes onto a Windows PC. Nous Research now ships Hermes as a Microsoft Store app alongside the desktop installer, the CLI, Docker and Hermes Cloud. Hermes is available as a Microsoft Store app for Windows.

What the Hermes Agent Microsoft Store app is
Hermes Agent is Nous Research’s free, open-source agent. The instruction for Store users is simple: it updates through the Store.




Hermes on Windows





Microsoft Store app
Installs from the Store and updates through the Store


Desktop installer
A .appinstaller file from the Hermes website that installs the signed MSIX bundle


CLI

The desktop packages bundle the agent, Python, the dependencies and the prebuilt interfaces, so the first launch doesn’t have to build anything. Nous’s docs note that Store packages have “separate Store ownership” from the website installer.

v0.22.1 (14 Oct) — a patch focused on Windows Store fixes.
v0.22.2 (15 Oct) — fixed the Store app sticking on “Connecting” and split the Store bundle into its own build lane.
v0.22.3 (21 Oct) — the Store build now goes live automatically when a release publishes.

Install and open Hermes Desktop.

The biggest barrier to AI agents for most people isn’t the AI — it’s the setup. A Store app with automatic updates removes the terminal, the Python installs and the “how do I update this?” problem. That puts a powerful agent in front of millions more Windows users.

items.content:
Hermes import agent is the one-command way to move into Hermes Agent without starting from scratch. hermes import-agent copies your setup from OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex CLI or — new in v0.22.4 on 21 October 2026 — Cursor. Here’s exactly what gets imported and how to do it safely.

Key takeaways

hermes import-agent imports from OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor.
Memories, rules, skills and MCP servers come across; keys stay behind by default.
It previews first and asks before changing anything.
--sync keeps Hermes up to date when the old agent changes. Claim a free strategy session for help.






What Hermes import agent does
The agent-importers plugin adds the hermes import-agent command. It reads the setup folder of another agent and writes the useful parts into your active Hermes profile. It always shows you a preview first and asks before applying anything.




Import from
Folder it reads




OpenClaw
~/.openclaw (or the older ~/.clawdbot and ~/.moltbot)


Claude Code
~/.claude


Codex CLI
~/.codex


Cursor
~/.cursor (new in v1.1.0, shipped with Hermes v0.22.4)




It used to be built into Hermes core. Now it’s an official plugin, and hermes setup offers to install it when it spots one of these agents on your machine.
Importing from Claude Code, Codex or Cursor

Instructions, Cursor rules and memories become Hermes memory entries.
Bash permission rules become Hermes command allow and deny lists.
MCP servers are added to Hermes’ config.yaml.
Skills are copied across.
--sync re-imports any source that has changed since last time.

That last one is handy if you keep using Claude Code or Cursor for coding: Hermes stays in step with the rules and memories you build there.

Migrating from OpenClaw to Hermes
For OpenClaw, the importer is the former hermes claw migrate command. It brings over your persona, memories, skills, model and messaging settings, MCP servers and agent behaviour — including workspace files like SOUL.md, MEMORY.md and USER.md.

API keys and bot tokens only come across if you add --migrate-secrets, and the preview lists which ones.
It creates a restore point (a pre-migration zip) and a migration report with backups.
It warns you if OpenClaw or a Hermes gateway is still running.
hermes claw cleanup renames your old OpenClaw folder after you confirm, so nothing is deleted.

Weighing up the switch? Read my Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw comparison first.
Is Hermes import agent safe?
Nous’s own notes on the plugin are reassuring. The importer makes no network calls and no model calls, so nothing leaves your machine. For Claude Code, Codex and Cursor it never reads their credential files, and it strips and lists any secret-looking MCP environment variables and headers. It writes only into your active Hermes profile, and it backs up your memory file before changing it.

Still review the preview carefully. Permission rules and MCP servers change what Hermes can do, so check you’re happy with every allow rule before you approve.

How to use Hermes import agent

Update Hermes: hermes update (the plugin needs Hermes v0.21.6+; Cursor support came with v0.22.4).
Install the plugin if hermes setup hasn’t already: hermes plugins install agent-importers.
Run hermes import-agent and read the preview.
Approve, then ask Hermes “what do you remember about me?” to check the import worked.
Add --sync later to pull in new changes.

Or skip the terminal: ask Hermes “import my Claude Code setup and show me the preview first”.
Why this matters for your business
Most people don’t switch agents because rebuilding everything is painful — months of rules, memories and skills are locked inside one tool. Hermes import agent removes that cost. You can try Hermes with everything you’ve already taught your other agents, and keep using both.
That’s the idea behind my Agent OS: use the best agent for each job, but give them one shared memory and one set of skills.

It helps to know the gaps before you switch:

Credentials from Claude Code, Codex and Cursor — never read, so log Hermes in to your providers yourself (Hermes can borrow Codex CLI and Claude Code logins).
OpenClaw keys and bot tokens — only with –migrate-secrets, and only allowlisted names.
Secret-looking MCP env vars and headers — stripped and listed so you can re-add them.
Your chat history — the importer moves setup, memories and skills, not old conversations.

Plan five minutes after the import to reconnect accounts and re-add any stripped secrets, and you’re done.
My verdict on Hermes import agent
It’s careful, previews everything and keeps backups. It also finally makes moving to Hermes painless for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenClaw users. If you’ve been putting off trying Hermes because of setup, run Hermes import agent and you’ll be up and running in minutes.

items.content:
Hermes Labs is a new home for experimental Hermes Agent plugins that Nous Research built but chose not to put in the core product. It arrived with Hermes Agent v0.22.4 on 21 October 2026, and it launched with three plugins: Inbox, Workflow Record and Telegram Business. All three install from the Hermes plugin catalog in one command. In the video below I walk through Hermes Mission Control and memory — the kind of “see everything your agent is doing” view that Hermes Labs’ Inbox plugin now gives you. Here’s what Hermes Labs is, what each plugin does, and whether you should use them.

Key takeaways

Hermes Labs = experimental plugins built by Nous Research but not officially supported.
Three plugins at launch: Inbox, Workflow Record and Telegram Business.
Each installs with hermes plugins install <name> from the community tier of the catalog.
Want help using them in your business? Claim a free strategy session.






What is Hermes Labs?
Hermes Labs is a GitHub repository from Nous Research called hermes-labs-plugins. Nous describes the plugins in it as Hermes features they decided not to add to the core. Rather than throw that work away, they released it so anyone who wants it can install it.
The catch is in the name. These are labs plugins, and Nous is clear that they are not supported:

No promise of fixes — a bug report may sit, and a core update could break a plugin before anyone notices.
Community tier — the plugin catalog lists them as community plugins, not official ones, so nobody thinks Nous maintains them.
Up for adoption — if you use one and want to own it, Nous will help you move it to your own repo.
Tested every night — CI runs each plugin against the current Hermes nightly build, so breakage is at least visible.

Supported, first-party plugins still live in hermes-official-plugins. Hermes Labs is the “works, but use at your own risk” shelf next to it.

hermes plugins install <plugin>




Hermes Labs plugin #1: Inbox
Install it with hermes plugins install inbox. Then hermes inbox shows everything in flight for your active profile in one read-only view:

Failed cron runs
Stalled or dropped delegations to sub-agents
Orphaned background processes
Blocked kanban tasks
Running work, undelivered results and upcoming jobs
Open chat sessions

If you run Hermes for real work, this is the one I’d install first. Once you have scheduled jobs, sub-agents and background tasks running, the hardest part is knowing what broke overnight. Inbox puts it all on one screen, and because it’s read-only it can’t change anything by accident.

Hermes Labs plugin #2: Workflow Record
Install it with hermes plugins install workflow-record. Then hermes record captures a browser workflow you demonstrate once — your clicks, the values you type into fields and the pages you visit. Passwords are masked inside the page.
The plugin ships with a skill that lets Hermes’ /learn command turn that recording into a skill Hermes can replay. In plain English: show Hermes a task once, and it learns to do it.
That’s a big deal for business owners, because most repetitive admin lives in a browser — filling in the same form, downloading the same report, posting to the same dashboard. Record it once, turn it into a skill, and hand it to your agent.
Hermes Labs plugin #3: Telegram Business
Install it with hermes plugins install hermes-telegram-business. It turns Hermes into an “observe-with-approval” secretary for your Telegram Business account. Hermes drafts replies to your customers, and nothing is sent until you approve it.
Telegram Business used to have its own repository. With v0.22.4 it moved into Hermes Labs’ community tier, so it now sits alongside the other experimental plugins.

items.content:
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Hermes is the pairing of NVIDIA’s newest local model with Hermes Agent. NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on 15 October 2026, and Hermes Agent v0.22.3 added it to Hermes’ local runtime on 21 October. Key takeaways

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: NVIDIA’s 74B-A9B model squeezed into 24GB.
Added to Hermes Agent’s local runtime in v0.22.3.
Text and image input, tool calling, up to 256K context (per Ollama).
Needs an NVIDIA GPU — Apple Silicon isn’t supported yet. Claim a free strategy session for help.






What is Nemotron 3.5 Bolt?
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt is part of NVIDIA’s open Nemotron family, announced alongside Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. NVIDIA says the 74B-A9B version uses native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 74 billion parameters in total and about 9 billion active per token, so it runs far faster than its size suggests.

#1 open model in its class on PinchBench, #2 among open models on BrowseComp

Hermes Agent v0.22 brought one-click local models, and the v0.22.3 release added Nemotron 3.5 Bolt (plus one-slot DFlash drafts, a speed-up feature) to Hermes’ local runtime. items.title: Hermes Agent Sandbox: Every Way to Run Hermes Safely (2026)
items.content:
Hermes Agent sandbox options decide where your agent’s commands actually run — straight on your computer, or inside a box that limits what it can touch. With v0.22.4 on 21 October 2026, Nous Research added a new Bubblewrap sandbox for Linux and moved Singularity/Apptainer into the plugin catalog. In the video below I show the Hermes plugin library these backends now install from. Here’s every Hermes sandbox option, what each one protects, and which one I’d choose.

Key takeaways

Hermes runs commands through a terminal backend — local, or a sandbox.
Options: Docker, SSH, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox, Singularity and Bubblewrap.
Bubblewrap is new: a lightweight Linux sandbox per command.
Switch with hermes config set terminal.backend <name> — or claim a free strategy session for help.






Why a Hermes Agent sandbox matters
Hermes is powerful because it can run real commands: install software, edit files, run scripts. That’s also the risk. On the default local backend, commands run directly on your machine with no isolation. A sandbox puts a wall between the agent and the things you care about — your SSH keys, cloud logins, personal files and the rest of your system.
Hermes already has other safety layers: dangerous-command approvals, your own deny rules (which apply to every backend), a file-write denylist and prompt-injection scanning. A sandbox adds the strongest one: even if something goes wrong, it happens inside the box.
Every Hermes Agent sandbox option




Backend
Where commands run
Good for




local
Your machine directly, no isolation
Development on a machine you trust


docker
A hardened Docker container (all Linux capabilities dropped by default)
Most people who want isolation


ssh
A remote server
Keeping the agent off your own computer


modal
A Modal cloud sandbox (direct or via the Nous gateway)
Cloud isolation without managing servers


daytona
A Daytona workspace

Hermes Agent sandbox options decide where your agent’s commands actually run — straight on your computer, or inside a box that limits what it can touch. With v0.22.4 on 21 October 2026, Nous Research added a new Bubblewrap sandbox for Linux and moved Singularity/Apptainer into the plugin catalog. In the video below I show the Hermes plugin library these backends now install from. Here’s every Hermes sandbox option, what each one protects, and which one I’d choose.

Key takeaways

Hermes runs commands through a terminal backend — local, or a sandbox.

Options: Docker, SSH, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox, Singularity and Bubblewrap.

Bubblewrap is new: a lightweight Linux sandbox per command.

Switch with hermes config set terminal.backend <name> — or claim a free strategy session for help.

Why a Hermes Agent sandbox matters

Hermes is powerful because it can run real commands: install software, edit files, run scripts. That’s also the risk. On the default local backend, commands run directly on your machine with no isolation. A sandbox puts a wall between the agent and the things you care about — your SSH keys, cloud logins, personal files and the rest of your system.

Hermes already has other safety layers: dangerous-command approvals, your own deny rules (which apply to every backend), a file-write denylist and prompt-injection scanning. A sandbox adds the strongest one: even if something goes wrong, it happens inside the box.
